Counterexamples and If and Only If

Demolish false claims with a single counterexample. Four plausible claims go on trial, one by one.

A 'for all' claim falls to one counterexample. A single failing case makes the whole claim false. An if-and-only-if claim is the opposite job. Each direction needs its own separate proof.

For example, take 'every 🧑 classmate wears glasses'. One classmate without glasses ends the claim. One person is enough.

Examples & Exercises

Counterexample

Disprove the claim "if n2n^2n2 is divisible by 4 then nnn is divisible by 4" using the counterexample n=2n = 2n=2. Write out the claim's logical form ∀n∈Z (4∣n2⇒4∣n)\forall n \in \mathbb{Z}\,(4 \mid n^2 \Rightarrow 4 \mid n)∀n∈Z(4∣n2⇒4∣n) and its negation ∃n∈Z (4∣n2 and 4∤n)\exists n \in \mathbb{Z}\,(4 \mid n^2 \text{ and } 4 \nmid n)∃n∈Z(4∣n2 and 4∤n) explicitly, and explain why a single witness settles the matter.

∀n∈Z (4∣n2⇒4∣n),¬(∀n∈Z P(n))=∃n∈Z ¬P(n)\forall n \in \mathbb{Z}\,(4 \mid n^2 \Rightarrow 4 \mid n),\qquad \lnot\Big(\forall n \in \mathbb{Z}\,P(n)\Big) = \exists n \in \mathbb{Z}\,\lnot P(n)∀n∈Z(4∣n2⇒4∣n),¬(∀n∈ZP(n))=∃n∈Z¬P(n)
n=2:n2=4,  4∣4,  but 4∤2n = 2:\quad n^2 = 4,\; 4 \mid 4,\; \text{but } 4 \nmid 2n=2:n2=4,4∣4,but 4∤2
Verdict

The claim is false — n=2n = 2n=2 is a counterexample (4∣224 \mid 2^24∣22 but 4∤24 \nmid 24∤2).

Show proof

Counterexample and verification

  1. The claim is a universal statement: ∀n∈Z (4∣n2⇒4∣n)\forall n \in \mathbb{Z}\,(4 \mid n^2 \Rightarrow 4 \mid n)∀n∈Z(4∣n2⇒4∣n) — the domain is n∈Zn \in \mathbb{Z}n∈Z.

    By the basic rules of logic its negation is the existential statement ∃n∈Z ¬(4∣n2⇒4∣n)\exists n \in \mathbb{Z}\,\lnot(4 \mid n^2 \Rightarrow 4 \mid n)∃n∈Z¬(4∣n2⇒4∣n), which by ¬(P⇒Q)=P∧¬Q\lnot(P \Rightarrow Q) = P \wedge \lnot Q¬(P⇒Q)=P∧¬Q equals ∃n∈Z (4∣n2∧4∤n)\exists n \in \mathbb{Z}\,(4 \mid n^2 \wedge 4 \nmid n)∃n∈Z(4∣n2∧4∤n).

    So it suffices to exhibit one n∈Zn \in \mathbb{Z}n∈Z for which the hypothesis is true and the conclusion false — and conversely, one such nnn is all it takes.

  2. Take n=2n = 2n=2.

    Then n2=4n^2 = 4n2=4 and 4∣44 \mid 44∣4, so the hypothesis is true.

    But n=2n = 2n=2 is not divisible by 4, so the conclusion 4∣n4 \mid n4∣n is false.

    Hence n=2n = 2n=2 is a witness to ∃n (4∣n2∧4∤n)\exists n\,(4 \mid n^2 \wedge 4 \nmid n)∃n(4∣n2∧4∤n), and the original universal claim is false.

    n=2:4∣n2=4 true,4∣2 false (i.e. 4∤2 true)⇒ counterexamplen = 2:\quad 4 \mid n^2 = 4\ \text{true},\qquad 4 \mid 2\ \text{false (i.e. } 4 \nmid 2\ \text{true)} \Rightarrow\ \text{counterexample}n=2:4∣n2=4 true,4∣2 false (i.e. 4∤2 true)⇒ counterexample

  3. Remark: checking a hundred values of nnn where the hypothesis trails the conclusion — e.g. n=4,8,12n = 4, 8, 12n=4,8,12 all work — never proves a universal claim.

    One counterexample outweighs infinitely many supporting cases.

    (The "fixed version" of this claim — nnn is even   ⟺  \iff⟺ n2n^2n2 is even — is proved in both directions in problem 2 below.)

Prove completely, in both directions, that nnn is even if and only if n2n^2n2 is even. Use a direct proof for the ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ direction (n=2kn = 2kn=2k gives n2=2(2k2)n^2 = 2(2k^2)n2=2(2k2)) and the contrapositive for the ⇐\Leftarrow⇐ direction (odd n=2k+1n = 2k+1n=2k+1 gives odd n2=2(2k2+2k)+1n^2 = 2(2k^2+2k)+1n2=2(2k2+2k)+1), and state explicitly why the two directions are different proofs.

n even  ⟺  n2 evenn\ \text{even} \iff n^2\ \text{even}n even⟺n2 even
⇒: n=2k  ⇒  n2=2(2k2),⇐: ¬(n even)⇒¬(n2 even)\Rightarrow:\ n = 2k \;\Rightarrow\; n^2 = 2(2k^2),\qquad \Leftarrow:\ \lnot(n\ \text{even}) \Rightarrow \lnot(n^2\ \text{even})⇒: n=2k⇒n2=2(2k2),⇐: ¬(n even)⇒¬(n2 even)
Show proof

  1. (⇒\Rightarrow⇒) Suppose nnn is even.

    Then n=2kn = 2kn=2k for some integer kkk.

    Squaring gives n2=4k2=2(2k2)n^2 = 4k^2 = 2(2k^2)n2=4k2=2(2k2), and since 2k22k^22k2 is an integer, n2n^2n2 is even.

    This is a direct proof — it starts from the assumption, unfolds the definition, and reaches the conclusion.

  2. (⇐\Leftarrow⇐) The reverse direction resists a direct proof: from the assumption "n2n^2n2 is even" there is no way to extract nnn.

    Prove the contrapositive instead: if nnn is odd then n2n^2n2 is odd.

    Write n=2k+1n = 2k+1n=2k+1; then n2=4k2+4k+1=2(2k2+2k)+1n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1n2=4k2+4k+1=2(2k2+2k)+1, and since 2k2+2k2k^2 + 2k2k2+2k is an integer, n2n^2n2 is odd.

    The contrapositive holds, so the original implication "n2n^2n2 even ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ nnn even" holds.

    (2k+1)2=4k2+4k+1=2(2k2+2k)+1 odd(2k+1)^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1\ \text{odd}(2k+1)2=4k2+4k+1=2(2k2+2k)+1 odd

  3. The two directions are genuinely different proofs: ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ unfolds the definition of even, n=2kn = 2kn=2k, directly, while ⇐\Leftarrow⇐ goes around it via the contrapositive.

    Proving only one direction establishes an implication, not an equivalence.

    To claim "P  ⟺  QP \iff QP⟺Q" both arrows are needed, and they usually require different arguments like this.

Prove that for real x,yx, yx,y, x2=y2x^2 = y^2x2=y2 holds if and only if x=yx = yx=y or x=−yx = -yx=−y. For the ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ direction use the factorization x2−y2=(x−y)(x+y)=0x^2 - y^2 = (x-y)(x+y) = 0x2−y2=(x−y)(x+y)=0 together with the zero-product property; for the ⇐\Leftarrow⇐ direction substitute directly in each case.

x2=y2  ⟺  (x=y or x=−y)x^2 = y^2 \iff (x = y\ \text{or}\ x = -y)x2=y2⟺(x=y or x=−y)
⇒: x2−y2=(x−y)(x+y)=0,⇐: (−y)2=y2\Rightarrow:\ x^2 - y^2 = (x-y)(x+y) = 0,\qquad \Leftarrow:\ (-y)^2 = y^2⇒: x2−y2=(x−y)(x+y)=0,⇐: (−y)2=y2
Show proof

  1. (⇒\Rightarrow⇒) Suppose x2=y2x^2 = y^2x2=y2.

    Subtracting y2y^2y2 from both sides gives x2−y2=0x^2 - y^2 = 0x2−y2=0, and factoring yields (x−y)(x+y)=0(x-y)(x+y) = 0(x−y)(x+y)=0.

    For real numbers, a product of two numbers is 0 only if one of them is 0 (divide by whichever factor is nonzero), so x−y=0x - y = 0x−y=0 or x+y=0x + y = 0x+y=0 — i.e. x=yx = yx=y or x=−yx = -yx=−y.

  2. (⇐\Leftarrow⇐) The reverse direction is checked directly in each case.

    If x=yx = yx=y then x2=y2x^2 = y^2x2=y2 is immediate, and if x=−yx = -yx=−y then x2=(−y)2=y2x^2 = (-y)^2 = y^2x2=(−y)2=y2.

    In both cases x2=y2x^2 = y^2x2=y2 holds.

  3. Remark: this biconditional explains the scene's counterexample — first prove ∣x∣=∣y∣  ⟺  x2=y2|x| = |y| \iff x^2 = y^2∣x∣=∣y∣⟺x2=y2 itself, in both directions.

    (⇒)(\Rightarrow)(⇒) If ∣x∣=∣y∣|x| = |y|∣x∣=∣y∣, squaring gives x2=∣x∣2=∣y∣2=y2x^2 = |x|^2 = |y|^2 = y^2x2=∣x∣2=∣y∣2=y2 (using ∣t∣2=t2|t|^2 = t^2∣t∣2=t2).

    (⇐)(\Leftarrow)(⇐) If x2=y2x^2 = y^2x2=y2 then ∣x∣2=∣y∣2|x|^2 = |y|^2∣x∣2=∣y∣2; since ∣x∣,∣y∣≥0|x|, |y| \ge 0∣x∣,∣y∣≥0 and squaring is injective (strictly increasing) on [0,∞)[0, \infty)[0,∞), it follows that ∣x∣=∣y∣|x| = |y|∣x∣=∣y∣.

    Hence ∣x∣=∣y∣|x| = |y|∣x∣=∣y∣ is equivalent to x2=y2x^2 = y^2x2=y2, so what is actually forced is not "x=yx = yx=y" but "x=yx = yx=y or x=−yx = -yx=−y".

    The scene's pairs (n,−n)(n, -n)(n,−n) are witnesses to the second alternative.

    This is the classic pattern: a counterexample shows how the claim must be repaired.
